line: Hi, we're Processors Assemble: Sarvesh, Aryan, Trishit, Husain, and I'm Navodit.
We built a RISC-V processor in Verilog, first single cycle, then as a five stage pipeline, to see how much faster pipelining really makes it.
On paper, five stages means five times faster. So we built three CPUs for the same 18 instructions to test that.
Single cycle, a pipeline without forwarding, and one with it. Same tests, same FPGA.
To compare them, we use the iron law: run time is instructions, times cycles per instruction, over the clock.
So a pipeline only wins if its cycles per instruction stay below its clock speedup. That bar is 1.94 without forwarding, and 1.43 with it.
Here's our starting point. In the single cycle CPU, every instruction finishes in one cycle, so the clock must wait for the slowest one, a load.
A load reads registers, uses the ALU, reads memory and writes back, all at once. That's 17 nanoseconds, or 58.75 megahertz.
To pipeline it, we cut that datapath into five stages, with registers in between, so five instructions are in flight at once.
The catch is they depend on each other. The green wires pass results back early. The red one throws away wrong work after a branch.
Structural hazards, two instructions fighting over hardware, we designed out completely.
Forwarding fixes almost every data hazard. The exception is a load whose result is used straight away. That costs one cycle.
And by the time a branch is taken, two wrong instructions have started, so we flush them.
All of this lives in one small module, the hazard unit.
This line spots the load case: a load, and the next instruction needs its result.
This one is the flush. Just a taken branch.
And this is the stall. With forwarding, only the load case. Without it, any result still on its way.
Forwarding checks the newest result first, so you always get the latest value.
Now let's see it run. make test runs every program on all three CPUs, and checks each against our Python reference simulator.
All 248 pass, in under three seconds.
make demo runs a program built to hit every hazard: seven instructions, 14 cycles, one stall, one flush. It also saves a waveform.
Here's forwarding. Both forward signals switch to 2, so the add gets x1 straight from the instruction ahead.
Here's the stall. The add right after the load waits one cycle for its value.
And the flush. The branch is taken, so the two instructions behind it are thrown away.
The same program as a pipeline diagram from the simulation: 14 cycles with forwarding, 19 without.
Without forwarding, an instruction waits until the result it needs is written back.
Every program must match the reference on all three CPUs: every register, every memory word, and the instruction count.
That's 248 automated checks, all passing.
So, is it faster? After place and route on a Lattice ECP5, pipelining nearly doubles the clock, from 58.75 to 113.86 megahertz.
Forwarding pulls it back to 83.89, because its extra logic sits right before the branch decision.
Without forwarding, the biggest loss is waiting on data. Forwarding removes them.
What's left is the load stall and branches, adding 0.23 to 0.35 cycles per instruction.
So the pipeline is only 0.71 to 1.29 times as fast. Nowhere near five.
The slowest path is still 52 percent of the single cycle one without forwarding, 70 percent with it. And every loop pays two cycles for its branch.
So a pipeline only wins when the clock it gains beats the cycles it loses.
In Phase II, we go after those two losses, branches and the long critical path, then add instructions and run on a real board. Thanks for watching.
